questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $p$ and $q$ are two statements, show that $p \Rightarrow q$ is logically equivalent to $\sim(p \wedge \sim q)$. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Two statements are logically equivalent if they have the same truth value for every assignment of truth values to $p$ and $q$. Build the truth table:

| $p$ | $q$ | $p \Rightarrow q$ | $\sim q$ | $p \wedge \sim q$ | $\sim(p \wedge \sim q)$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | F | F | T |
| T | F | F | T | T | F |
| F | T | T | F | F | T |
| F | F | T | T | F | T |

The columns for $p \Rightarrow q$ and $\sim(p \wedge \sim q)$ are identical, so the two statements are logically equivalent.

Algebraic confirmation: by De Morgan's law, $\sim(p \wedge \sim q) \equiv \sim p \vee \sim(\sim q) \equiv \sim p \vee q$, and $p \Rightarrow q$ is false only when $p$ is true and $q$ is false, i.e. $p \Rightarrow q \equiv \sim p \vee q$.
$$\boxed{p \Rightarrow q \;\equiv\; \sim(p \wedge \sim q)}$$

questions.enonce_markdown: The function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is given by $f(x) = 2x^3 + 3x - 2$. Show that $f$ is monotonic increasing. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
$f$ is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$ with
$$f'(x) = 6x^2 + 3.$$
Since $x^2 \ge 0$ for all real $x$, $f'(x) \ge 3 > 0$ for every $x \in \mathbb{R}$. A differentiable function with positive derivative everywhere is (strictly) increasing: $x_1 < x_2 \Rightarrow f(x_1) < f(x_2)$. Hence $f$ is monotonic increasing on $\mathbb{R}$. $\blacksquare$

questions.enonce_markdown: The function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is given by $f(x) = 2x^3 + 3x - 2$. Deduce that the equation $f(x) = 0$ has a root within the interval $0 < x < 1$. Taking $x = 0.5$ as first approximation to the root of the equation $f(x) = 0$, use Newton-Raphson's method once to obtain, to 2 decimal places, a second approximation to the root of this equation. (5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Existence of the root.** $f$ is a polynomial, hence continuous on $[0, 1]$. We have
$$f(0) = -2 < 0, \qquad f(1) = 2 + 3 - 2 = 3 > 0.$$
$f(0)$ and $f(1)$ have opposite signs, so by the intermediate value theorem there is a value $x$ with $0 < x < 1$ and $f(x) = 0$. Because $f$ is monotonic increasing (part (a)), it takes the value $0$ only once, so this root is the only real root.

**Newton-Raphson.** The iteration is $x_{n+1} = x_n - \dfrac{f(x_n)}{f'(x_n)}$ with $f'(x) = 6x^2 + 3$. For $x_1 = 0.5$:
$$f(0.5) = 2(0.125) + 1.5 - 2 = -0.25, \qquad f'(0.5) = 6(0.25) + 3 = 4.5.$$
$$x_2 = 0.5 - \frac{-0.25}{4.5} = 0.5 + \frac{1}{18} = \frac59 \approx 0.5556.$$
$$\boxed{x_2 \approx 0.56 \ \text{(2 d.p.)}}$$
(The actual root is $\approx 0.5536$, so $0.56$ is a good second approximation.)
